questions.question_text: A quadrilateral park $ABCD$ is divided by the diagonal $AC$ into two triangles. In triangle $ABC$, $AB=40$ m, $BC=55$ m and the angle at $B$ is $70^{\circ}$. In triangle $ACD$, $AD=43$ m, $DC=29$ m and the angle at $D$ is $100^{\circ}$. Find the total area of the park, correct to the nearest square metre.

options.why: Found the area of triangle $ABC$ only and did not add triangle $ACD$.
Found the area of triangle $ACD$ only and did not add triangle $ABC$.
Left out the $\tfrac12$ in both triangles, doubling the total.

questions.solution_text:
$A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$
Triangle $ABC$: $\dfrac{1}{2}(40)(55)\sin 70^{\circ}\approx 1033.7\text{ m}^{2}$
Triangle $ACD$: $\dfrac{1}{2}(43)(29)\sin 100^{\circ}\approx 614.0\text{ m}^{2}$
Total $=1033.7+614.0\approx 1\,648\text{ m}^{2}$

questions.question_text: Two sides of a triangular garden are $16$ m and $9$ m. As the included angle changes, what is the greatest possible area of the garden?

options.why: Left out the $\tfrac12$, computing $ab$ at the maximum.
Assumed the largest angle $180^{\circ}$ gives the largest area, but $\sin 180^{\circ}=0$.
Assumed a $60^{\circ}$ angle rather than the $90^{\circ}$ that maximises $\sin C$.

questions.solution_text:
$A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C=\dfrac{1}{2}(16)(9)\sin C$
$\sin C$ is greatest when $C=90^{\circ}$, where $\sin C=1$.
$A=\dfrac{1}{2}(16)(9)(1)=72\text{ m}^{2}$
